column1: Developments on data.gouv.fr are done in an agile manner and are primarily guided by:
1. User Feedback
The platform is primarily built based on user feedback
column2: which comes from several sources:

column1: - User tests and interviews
- Interviews serve to:
- Conduct forward-looking research and update the vision: maintaining a broad view of the users' context
column2: their needs
column3: sector evolution
column4: and usage trends
column5: rather than focusing solely on ongoing and planned work.

column1: - Prepare for a future project that hasn't been tackled yet
column2: to understand current usage
column3: identify user problems
column4: gather test data
column5: and validate or invalidate proposed features.

column1: - Tests serve to:
- Identify usability issues before coding
column2: understand how the application is used
column3: and detect its shortcomings.

column1: - Test planned changes at a lower cost using more or less finished and interactive mockups before coding.
- Verify
column2: once the changes are in production
column3: whether they work ""as expected"".

column1: Both approaches are essential for prioritizing upcoming work
column2: limiting the influence of personal biases. Ideally
column3: multiple elements or hypotheses are tested during a session with a user (as organizing it is time-consuming)
column4: and an ""interview"" part is included in the tests (with questions beyond what's on the screen).

column1: - Support feedback
- Feedback received by the support team
The support team is in direct contact with users and regularly receives valuable feedback. However
column2: it's important to note that this feedback mostly comes from data producers
column3: who represent only a portion of our users and whose needs may sometimes conflict with those of data reusers.

column1: - GitHub tickets
Some users
column2: often advanced users or partners
column3: propose improvements via GitHub.

column1: - Feedback from social media and specialized platforms
Insights can often be gleaned from community discussions on platforms like teamopendata
column2: Twitter
column3: or LinkedIn. However
column4: it's crucial to ensure the representativeness of this feedback compared to the rest of our users to avoid responding only to the loudest voices.

column1: 2. Usage Metrics
We monitor usage metrics
column2: such as platform activity (views
column3: downloads
column4: data previews) and catalog evolution (data quality improvement
column5: resource type evolution)
column6: to identify trends and ensure that our actions are heading in the right direction. However
column7: we place greater importance on impact indicators (see below).

column1: 3. Team Feedback
The team is also a critical source for prioritization. While user feedback and usage should remain our guiding star
column2: it's crucial to consider team feedback
column3: especially for:

column1: - Understanding the complexity and technical debt induced by developments
- Facilitating the work of the team (both the development team and the support team)
- Building a shared vision and ensuring team motivation
4. Other Types of Feedback
data.gouv.fr operates in a complex environment where feedback and directives can come from many sources (political mandates
column2: ministries
column3: management
column4: European partners). This feedback must also be carefully considered and sometimes addressed strategically
column5: even if it doesn't align perfectly with the product vision.

column1: This working methodology does not prevent data.gouv.fr from having a roadmap.
The roadmap of data.gouv.fr serves as a guiding thread for the team and facilitates interactions with stakeholders. The team aims to be agile
column2: so the roadmap is not set in stone and is not tied to specific dates or fixed deliverables.

column1: Mission and Impact Objectives
Above all
column2: the team pursues a mission and impact objectives.

column1: Our mission is to promote the reuse of public data. This mission is broken down into objectives and impact indicators.
1. Improve the discoverability of open data
2. Promote the quality of open data
3. Encourage the reuse of open data
Rituals
In practice
column2: it is the product owner's responsibility to synthesize needs and represent the user's voice within the team.

column1: We work in two-week sprints
column2: where we plan the tasks to be completed.

column1: The goal is to assume deliberate prioritization by asking
column2: what evolution of the application will bring the most value to the user at this moment? This also involves saying no regularly (or
column3: at worst
column4: ""later"") to protect the interests of both the user and the team
column5: and ultimately to ensure that we remain aligned with the product vision.

column1: We also strive to design features that are as ""small"" as possible.
The larger a feature or evolution is:
- the more likely we are to get stuck in an endless tunnel
- the more bugs we'll have to deal with
- the longer it will take to put into production
column2: delaying value delivery to the user

column1: - the longer it will take to get feedback on usage
- the higher the risk of having worked for nothing
We also aim to have the shortest feedback loop possible: changes are rolled out quickly because they are small and non-parallelized
column2: tests are systematic
column3: and usage and impact are measured. All of this helps us learn as quickly as possible whether the change effectively improves the product
column4: and to gain more insight into user behavior
column5: their expectations
column7: and ultimately to learn how to improve the product."

column1: This definition stems from the Code of Relations between the Public and the Administration : “Public information contained in documents communicated or published by the administrations mentioned in the first paragraph of article L. 300-2 may be used by any person who wishes to do so for purposes other than those of the public service mission for which the documents were produced or received.” (https://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/codes/article_lc/LEGIARTI000033219044). This definition is similar to the PSI Directive definition : “Public sector bodies collect
column2: produce

column1: The complexity and the need to clarify the definition of reuse has been emphasised in the literature
column2: particularly with respect to research data
column3: a key issue being the distinction between use and reuse.

column1: Besides that definition
column2: more restrictive approaches have also emerged : some consider that only perennial uses of data are reuses while others consider any use of data as reuse.

column1: In our day to day operations
column2: any exploitation of data in order to obtain information is considered as reuse
